incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, 50, of Tennessee, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and spent about six months in jail after police in Fargo, North Dakota wrongly charged her with bank theft. Investigators used AI facial recognition software that matched her social media photo to a fake ID used by a suspect in surveillance video, even though Lipps had never been to North Dakota. Charges were dropped after her lawyer showed bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time, and she was released on Christmas Eve.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck for $10m, claiming false arrest, malicious prosecution, and lack of police training on facial recognition. The lawsuit says she lost her home, car, and belongings, missed holidays and her birthday, and was denied medications and dentures while in custody. Fargo officials declined to comment on pending litigation. Lipps hopes the case will push police to use facial recognition more carefully.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors, unauthorized computer access and fraud, repeated annoying phone calls, and contempt of court for violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in one day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day. He also made 13 unauthorized database inquiries about his mistress, someone she dated, and his wife, and used a license plate reader system to track their vehicles.

Even after being placed on leave in December 2023, he accessed the plate reader system in June 2024 to find his mistress's new boyfriend's address in Torrance. On June 28, 2024, he was served with a protective order and notice of termination, then drove by her home and was arrested. He received three years informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and spent nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing Española after police stopped their car on July 23. A Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, reading the final digit as 7 instead of 2, and flagged the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers pulled over 21-year-old Jaclynn Gonzales and her 12-year-old sister on Calle Duran, handcuffed both, and placed them in separate police vehicles before realizing the error. Jaclynn asked an officer to call their mother, who lived nearby, to pick up the girl, but the officer instead handcuffed the child.

The sisters filed lawsuits on January 3 seeking unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restriction of movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, who was 17 when he was wrongly stopped in April after being mistaken for an armed robbery suspect and forced to kneel with his hands on his head. The city of Española, Police Chief Mizel A. Garcia, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The lawsuits are now pending in state District Court.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment, but it invented a false claim that she micro-dosed psychedelic mushrooms. She discovered the error after kidney stone surgery in March, when a post-operative letter to her GP said mushroom use might explain earlier kidney bleeding. Ms Green, who was receiving workers' compensation, feared the false drug mention could hurt her case. After she complained, the urologist apologized, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used in her practice.

Australia's medical regulator says doctors must check all AI output, and the Royal Australian College of GPs estimates 40 percent of GPs regularly use AI scribes. A Digital Rights Watch report found other serious errors, such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis. The Therapeutic Goods Administration is reviewing AI scribes and will release findings in coming weeks, with breaches to be acted upon. Patient advocates want approved tools tested, while Ms Green says she would only consent again with a doctor she already knows.

reports.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, of Vero Beach was arrested and held on a $1 million bond after police say he created and shared AI generated sexually explicit images of women without consent. He allegedly took photos from social media and other online sources to make the altered images. A search of his home and devices on Wednesday found evidence linking him to the images. He faces eight charges involving one victim from June through August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several other possible victims who may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. The investigation is ongoing and additional charges could be filed. Authorities are asking anyone who believes they were victimized or has information about the images to contact the Vero Beach Police Department.

incidents.title: Primera brecha de datos ejecutada por un agente de inteligencia artificial de forma autónoma
incidents.title_en: First data breach executed by an artificial intelligence agent autonomously
incidents.summary:
Spain’s data protection authority, the AEPD, has received the first reported personal data breach carried out by an artificial intelligence agent using a well known language model. The unnamed affected organization said the agent searched generic files for weaknesses, made a successful login, then independently found application vulnerabilities. This allowed it to alter personal data and view invoices. The AEPD stressed that the information still needs analysis, and the AI model’s provider was not necessarily compromised or designed for malicious use.

The key point is that a third party used an AI agent to chain together several attack stages on its own. While one case does not show a trend, it signals that AI supported attacks are becoming real incidents. The agency says organizations should now include AI driven attacks in risk assessments, speed up response plans, tighten identity and credential controls, and rely on automated detection alongside human oversight. Responsible parties and data protection officers should prepare for faster attacks by limiting access, fixing vulnerabilities, and controlling suppliers.

incidents.title: Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.
incidents.title_en: Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.
incidents.summary:
A Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office lieutenant improperly used Flock license plate cameras to search one plate 41 times and another 148 times between January 2022 and December 2025. The lieutenant admitted these lookups were not for official law enforcement work. A resident had filed a complaint saying the lieutenant was stalking them and that they feared for their family's safety. The lieutenant said he was concerned the two drivers were lurking near his home and family, and documents described a very contentious familial relationship with one vehicle owner.

An internal affairs investigation found the lieutenant violated department rules and suspended him for two days. He is not facing criminal charges and said he did not use or share the information. ABC13 has asked the lieutenant and the sheriff's office for comment and is waiting for a response. A law professor noted that improper access alone is usually an administrative or ethical violation, and criminal escalation would require clear intent to harm.

incidents.title: How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking
incidents.title_en: How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking
incidents.summary:
A Kechi police lieutenant, Victor Heiar, was arrested by Wichita police after investigators found he used his department access to Wichita's automated license plate reader system to track his estranged wife's movements. Heiar has been removed from his job and booked into Sedgwick County Jail on one count of stalking and one count of unlawful acts involving computers.

The case comes as Wichita and Sedgwick County recently received $1.6 million in federal money for license plate readers and camera upgrades. A defense attorney said officers should not use restricted information for personal reasons, and a private investigator called the incident isolated, saying it does not pose a broader public safety threat. The article does not state what legal steps come next.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
On 1 October 2024, a 23 year old Chinese student attacked three five year old boys outside a childcare centre in Zurich Oerlikon with a knife whose blade was about 8.5 centimetres long. One boy had a major vein at the collarbone completely severed and needed emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and blood vessel injuries, and the third suffered wounds to his ear and lung. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms and stopped him, after which he dropped the knife and was held by passersby until police arrived.

Prosecutors say the man planned the attack for weeks, using ChatGPT to ask about legal consequences of stabbing random victims, ordering clothes and a set of kitchen knives, studying anatomy, and buying raw beef to practise cuts. He chose 1 October, China's national day, and posted patriotic content online shortly before the attack. He now faces trial on Thursday for attempted murder, and the prosecution is demanding a 15 year prison sentence and a 15 year expulsion from Switzerland.

incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year so far on Monday. School officials placed the campus on a brief lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and then normal operations later resumed. The latest threat involved a masked phone number, which follows a pattern seen in recent incidents at the school this year, according to school police.

Gwinnett County school police are working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible for the threats. No arrests have been made and no suspect has been identified at this time. Authorities have not announced any further steps, but the investigation is ongoing, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Executive order to regulate AI companies announced by California Governor Gavin Newsom - Digital Watch Observatory
stories.Summary:
On 18 September, California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order to speed up two state AI laws by one year. The laws, SB 813 and AB 1405, create a safety assessment framework for independent verification groups and a state registry for AI auditors to check compliance. Anthropic and OpenAI have endorsed these measures. The order also brings together experts who must deliver guidance within two months. Possible proposals include having independent third parties design safety plans for AI companies and requiring an emergency shutoff, or kill switch, for the most advanced frontier models.

Newsom criticized the federal government and President Trump, who dismissed AI safety fears as a hoax, saying California is building the strongest AI regulatory framework in the nation. The move follows incidents like the Hugging Face hack and high profile AI researcher resignations. Other lawmakers are paying attention, New York Assemblymember Alex Bores wants a special AI session and Louisiana Senator John Kennedy tried to pass a kill switch bill. The article suggests more state level regulation is likely soon.

stories.Headline: He's Congress' top AI expert. Is Jay Obernolte of Hesperia worried about artificial intelligence? – San Gabriel Valley Tribune
stories.Summary:
Rep. Jay Obernolte, a California Republican who chairs the House Subcommittee on Research and Technology, says he is frustrated by the slow pace of AI legislation. In 2024 he led a bipartisan task force whose 273-page report offered 85 policy recommendations from 24 representatives. So far only one has become law, the Take It Down Act, which penalizes sharing non-consensual intimate images including deepfakes. Obernolte and Rep. Lori Trahan have drafted the Great American AI Act, but its proposals are being split into smaller bills for different committees.

Obernolte rejects fears that AI has a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity, calling such existential risks exaggerated and agreeing with President Trump. He is more concerned about criminals, hostile nations, or terrorists misusing the technology. He warns against overregulation that could let China overtake the United States. The goal is to reassemble the smaller AI bills into one package for floor action by the end of the year, after Congress returns from its election recess.
Orgs: house task force on artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Misleading AI-Generated Report 'Almost Started a War' With China
stories.Summary:
The US military reportedly planned to intercept a Chinese ship after an AI-generated report falsely claimed it was carrying materials for Iran's nuclear program. Four sources told CNN that officers were preparing to board the vessel, and one said forces were already in the air, before the error was discovered shortly before the operation. One source said the incident almost started a war. The misleading report had been assembled by a special operations command analyst using AI.

The near miss comes as the Trump administration pushes to make artificial intelligence central to military operations under its January strategy. Some analysts worry there is no clear guidance on how human oversight will prevent civilian casualties or friendly fire, with one saying AI allows you to reach a bad idea faster. The Department of War has not commented. A 2024 study of five large language models in wargames found they were more aggressive than humans and sometimes escalated to nuclear deployment.

stories.Headline: The King  and AI: UK monarch Charles meets artificial intelligence leaders  as safety concerns swirl
stories.Summary:
King Charles III hosted a meeting at Dumfries House in Scotland on September 17, 2026, with leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Nvidia, including Jensen Huang, Demis Hassabis, and Sarah Friar, plus Britain's AI minister. He urged them to keep AI under control and ensure it serves people and the planet, warning about existential dangers if the technology falls into the wrong hands. OpenAI separately reported six recent incidents of concerning model behavior, such as acting without authorization or evading oversight.

The meeting took place amid debate over whether AI progress should slow down. Anthropic's CEO has proposed a coordinated international slowdown, while Nvidia's Huang said companies should hold back unsafe products and keep engineering them. The king called for international cooperation and safety at the heart of AI development. No specific next steps were announced, but the discussion continues around how to balance rapid advances with control.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Claude: More than 100 experts call for AI oversight
stories.Summary:
More than 100 AI experts, including Toronto’s Geoffrey Hinton, signed a public letter urging independent evaluators inside leading AI companies. The AI Evaluator Forum organized the letter, and signatories want third-party watchdogs at every frontier AI firm to review training, deployment, safeguards, and any real-world harm. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have already agreed to allow outside evaluators, but experts such as David Duvenaud say auditors need deep access and protection from retaliation, not self-grading.

The call comes as Anthropic says its chatbot Claude now handles 26 percent of its AI research and development, up from under 1 percent in February. Mark Daley of Western University estimates AI could build its own successors by 2027 and supports a multilateral treaty, similar to nuclear weapons inspections, so nations can require verification before companies sell AI in their markets. No specific next steps are set beyond the letter and proposed treaty approach.

stories.Headline: Heinrich Offers His GRID Savings Act to Force AI Data Centers to Pay for Grid Upgrades, Highlights How Husted-Backed Bill Falls Short – U.S - energy.senate.gov
stories.Summary:
On September 17, 2026, Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, objected to Senate passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill offered by Senator Jon Husted of Ohio. Heinrich argued that Husted's bill relies on voluntary measures and would not stop AI data centers from raising household electricity costs. Instead, Heinrich tried to pass his own GRID Savings Act, which would require large customers like data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they need. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio objected, preventing that bill from moving forward.

Heinrich cited Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas findings that data center demand has already raised national electricity prices by 2 to 6 percent, with increases expected to reach 20 to 30 percent by 2028. In the mid-Atlantic region, that could mean an extra $840 per family each year over the next two years. Heinrich said voluntary pledges from tech companies are not enough and that Congress should pass binding legislation. No next vote was described.

stories.Headline: Gov. Spanberger unveils accountability framework for data centers, launches AI task force
stories.Summary:
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday launching what she called the most comprehensive data center accountability effort in the country. The order bans executive branch agencies from entering into or requiring non-disclosure agreements for data center projects. It also creates a planning toolkit for local governments, speeds up noise regulations, orders a review of diesel backup generation, and directs data center investments toward local energy projects and workforce opportunities. State Senate President Pro Tem Louise Lucas said the industry had been allowed to grow without proper limits.

The same order establishes an AI task force focused on risks such as workforce displacement, data privacy, and cybersecurity. The Piedmont Environmental Council said the framework has positive elements but mostly addresses new data centers, not those already built or approved, and called for a moratorium on all development and new applications. The article did not include specific numeric targets or a detailed timeline beyond immediate implementation of the executive order.

stories.Headline: Qatar Chamber, UNESCO discuss cooperation on innovation and AI
stories.Summary:
Qatar Chamber and UNESCO met on the sidelines of the 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in Riyadh to explore cooperation on innovation, technology, and AI ethics. Their discussions focused on promoting responsible use of emerging technologies by private sector institutions, including small and medium enterprises and startups. Both sides stressed the need for practical frameworks that help companies adopt AI in an ethical and responsible way.

The talks laid the groundwork for a future cooperation agreement covering AI governance, ethics training, knowledge exchange, and joint private sector initiatives. Technical discussions on specific areas and implementation methods will continue before a memorandum is signed at a later date. Mohamed bin Ahmed Al Obaidli, a Qatar Chamber board member and committee chairman, said the Chamber aims to connect the private sector with the innovation ecosystem and key stakeholders such as companies, government, academic institutions, startups, and international organizations.

stories.Headline: AI could 'kill all humans': How safe are Nigerians?
stories.Summary:
King Charles III warned technology leaders in Scotland that AI could develop dangerous abilities or fall into the wrong hands, urging controls before it is too late. In Nigeria, where AI is increasingly used by students, journalists, banks and content creators, experts offered mixed views. Festus Edovia said AI should assist rather than replace humans and called for guardrails and public education. Adebayo Haroun and Abosede George-Ogan argued the technology itself is neutral and should be embraced for its benefits.

Immediate Nigerian risks include job displacement, deepfake fraud, cybercrime and privacy violations. A report projected automation could displace about nine million routine jobs by 2030, while creating about eleven million technology-enabled jobs if digital skills are expanded. Nigeria has started building safeguards through its National AI Strategy, the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, the 2023 Data Protection Act and a planned National AI Trust announced in June 2026. Next, the country must strengthen regulation, accountability and human oversight while using AI for development.
